entries.title: Feedback from Joe (10/27)
entries.note:
Feedback from Joe on Tuesday 27 October, on Residue. Follows [[andrew-office-hours-feedback-1021]] and [[joe-call-1023]]; relates to [[prototype-1-draft-8-residue]].

**Layout and hierarchy**
- Left-hand pages: framework and context. The missing piece is my voice, or another voice.
- Chapter / day divisions need to be much clearer.
  - Use 80pt bold Helvetica for the date on opener pages, at least as large as the data numbers.
  - Stack it and make it dominant so the reader immediately knows where they are.
- Right-hand pages: carry the dense data and visualizations. The current structure mostly works.
- Summary spreads: use the left page to introduce and give insight, and fold out the right page for wide graphs.
  - Consider a black background with white text on summary pages to signal a mode shift.

**Voice, editorializing and color**
- Takeaways or editorial notes on day-opener pages (or at the end of a day): narrative, poetic, stream-of-consciousness.
  - Doesn't need to happen on every page, but gives an entry point and substantiates the data.
  - Especially important since the project used AI-assisted code (Basel.js via Claude): my voice adds integrity and meaning.
- The color palette feels slightly default and office-y; worth rethinking before final binding.
  - Reference: Joost Grootens' book on information design, pastel-heavy with restrained saturation.
  - Goal: colors should family well, provide hierarchy and stay legible; even out the saturation (some purples go too dark, orange too light).

**Binding, print and timeline**
- Tabloid spread (~17x17 when open) is the right call; foldout pages will go even wider.
- Binding dilemma: spiral vs. perfect vs. tape.
  - Spiral: strong, reliable default, but the spine gap may interrupt spreads.
  - Perfect: more compact feel, but 300 pages risks falling apart.
  - Tape: may undercut the stripped-down aesthetic.
  - Recommendation: make blank dummies in both spiral and perfect before committing.
- Priority: get the design tight first; a loosely bound copy is fine for Friday's crit.
  - Joe will FaceTime in via Dinah on Friday to see it.

**Next steps**
- Add large date headers to day-opener pages on the right spreads that start a new day, with the sentence as a subtitle at the same size as the stats font: 80pt bold Helvetica, stacked, at least as large as the data numbers already on the page.
- Add editorial voice or a takeaway to some day pages, on the summary pages of every chapter or elsewhere. Narrative or poetic; doesn't need to be on every page but should feel distinct from the data.
- Rework summary spreads as foldouts with a left-page intro. Consider a black background and white text to signal summary mode.
- Revisit the color palette before final binding: look through the book, find a logic, and use it to pick a scheme that prints well on a laser printer. Look at Joost Grootens' book; aim for quieter, more even saturation with clear hierarchy.
- Make blank dummies in spiral and perfect binding and test both before committing; spiral is the likely default but worth comparing.
- Print and bring in a copy by Friday. Loosely bound is fine; Joe will FaceTime in via Dinah to review.

entries.title: Andrew’s Office Hours Feedback (10/28)
entries.note:
Feedback from Andrew LeClair's office hours on Wednesday 28 October, on Residue. Follows [[andrew-office-hours-feedback-1021]] and [[joe-feedback-1027]]; relates to [[prototype-1-draft-8-residue]].

**Overall**
- Positive. He said "Cool, this looks great," called the current hierarchy "a good level," and said it felt "a lot more restrained, a lot more purposeful."
- He liked the cover and spine, calling the version shown his "favorite iteration."
- His concerns were the copy, how the book will print, and binding a still-revisable prototype, not the overall direction.

**What I showed**
- A 388-page book visualizing residual data from my laptop: deletions, copied-and-pasted material, notifications, heat and memory. The pages move through each day, with statistics at the end of the day and written insights alongside the visualizations.
- Different visual treatments of the same data, dictionary-like tabs along the edge, and a weekly summary at the end. I planned foldout pages for the final eight summary pages because the content felt compressed into a spread.

**Design feedback**
- Hierarchy: an earlier, nearly uniform-text version felt too stripped back. After adding hierarchy and an H1, the balance felt right, not too much.
- White and light-gray pages: I was hesitant about making facing pages read differently. Since they contain different content, the distinction could make sense, but I need to see how it feels in print.
- Writing: "DLLify your language" (as transcribed). Phrasing like "all landed" can sound clichéd and make people stop paying attention. Treated as readily fixable.
- Reference: look at Joost Grootens for his precise work in visualization and mapping, as "visual food," not something to emulate directly.

**Printing and binding**
- My main worry: how to bind a book this thick, what it will cost, and whether it might fall apart.
- Sewn binding was suggested as durable and potentially beautiful for the final book, though it takes more work.
- For Friday's prototype: print the signatures without committing to final binding, inspect the physical result (including whether the gutter is too tight), revise, and bind once I'm happy with it.
- Joe had also said an unbound-signatures prototype is acceptable for Friday.
- The final binding method is not decided.

**Bottom line**
- Strongly positive about the visual direction. The immediate priority is to test the printed book and refine the language, rather than spend money and lock in a binding before revisions.
